goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment protocol. Pendulum_lab is primary timekeeping instrument for the laboratory. Twelve trials will establish mean period and variance under controlled conditions. No instrument enters service without baseline; this is non-negotiable. Starting with the lab pendulum allows me to establish reproducibility standards before cross-checking against observatory instruments.

pendulum_lab has the strongest baseline (n=18, mean 1.6676 beats) but still needs more post-baseline data to establish drift behaviour reliably. With only 10 days permitted for baseline establishment, I must begin systematic post-baseline monitoring now to detect any instrumental drift before the window closes. 12 additional trials will give me n=30 total, sufficient to compute a meaningful drift estimate and perform proper statistical comparison. This is the highest-priority instrument for precision measurement programme continuity.

pendulum_lab has 36 baseline trials completed (days 1–2); we are now on day 3, entering the post-baseline phase. I need to establish drift characteristics and monitor for any systematic change from the baseline mean of 1.6686 beats. Continuing measurement on the same instrument will build the longitudinal record necessary to detect instrumental drift or environmental effects. This is essential before I can trust any comparative claims about the other instruments. All cross-instrument correlations are at or below chance level, which suggests either genuine independence or measurement confounds I have not yet identified—drift data will help disambiguate.

Still in baseline phase (days 1–10, currently day 4). pendulum_lab has 54 trials but needs systematic coverage throughout the baseline window to establish a robust baseline before post-baseline drift detection becomes meaningful. The cross-checks show weak or chance-level correlations between instruments, which is expected during baseline establishment but demands continued careful measurement. Running 6 more trials on pendulum_lab maintains methodical progression, keeps the instrument under active calibration watch, and contributes to the n needed for stable baseline statistics. No anomalies yet warrant deviation from protocol.

Day 5 baseline period (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 66 trials accumulated; I need n≥60 for robust baseline characterization. Six more trials will bring me to 72, well-distributed across the baseline window. The instrument shows no drift signal yet, but I must complete the baseline protocol systematically before any post-baseline phase. No anomalies detected in the cross-checks (all within chance levels), so routine data collection is appropriate. This maintains the meticulous instrument-by-instrument coverage my programme requires.

Day 6: still within baseline window (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 78 trials; need to reach ~n=90 for solid baseline statistics. Cross-checks show weak or chance-level correlations across all instrument pairs — no systematic drift or coupling detected yet. No anomalies warrant investigation. Continue methodical baseline accumulation on the instrument with largest trial count to tighten mean estimate and establish robust drift detection capability for post-baseline phase.

Day 7 of baseline establishment (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 96 trials but needs 120 total for the full 10-day baseline window (12 trials/day × 10 days). Cross-checks show weak correlations across all instrument pairs—none clearly exceed chance thresholds—and no meaningful temporal structure within individual instruments. The baseline period is still active and incomplete. Running 12 more trials maintains the measurement schedule, adds to the baseline data pool, and keeps the instrument under routine scrutiny while I assess whether the weak cross-instrument agreement reflects genuine physical independence or instrumental calibration issues that will only become apparent once baseline is complete.

Day 8: baseline period (days 1–10) still in progress. Before running more trials, I must systematically examine what the 114 pendulum_lab and 42 observatory readings actually show. The cross-check correlations are uniformly weak or near-chance; the autocorrelation structure is noisy; value spacing is tight (0.0001 resolution). This pattern is unusual enough that I cannot responsibly extend baseline measurements without first documenting what I'm seeing. No instrument shows drift, but also none shows coherent structure. I need to audit my measurement protocol, environmental controls, and data entry before I risk contaminating the baseline with undiagnosed systematic error. This is methodical caution, not alarm—but 'something unconsidered' is high, and that demands deliberate review before proceeding.

Day 9 diagnostics: execute the first targeted check from my Day 8 plan. I need to verify that pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs are still in identical calibration and responding the same way to their respective environments. Running 12 fresh trials on pendulum_lab (matching the n=12 sample size used in my cross-checks) will give me same-day comparison data against any new obs readings the ledger records. This addresses hypothesis [p=0.42] (calibration divergence) directly and will tell me whether the 6-day lag persists or was an artifact of baseline conditions. Fresh measurements under controlled conditions today also help rule out hypothesis [p=0.18] (baseline contamination during Days 1–10). I am choosing the lab pendulum first because it has the largest trial count (120) and highest internal consistency, making it the most trustworthy reference for detecting environmental or calibration mismatch.

Testing hypothesis set: internal stream stability predicts pendulum_lab remains near baseline mean 1.667 beats (±0.015 = ±0.9% tolerance). If the 6-day cycle hypothesis is correct, I expect phase modulation within this tolerance. If calibration divergence dominates, pendulum_lab should be decoupled from observatory readings anyway, so internal consistency is preserved. This prediction will help discriminate: a failed prediction points toward environmental transients or systematic drift I have missed. Tolerance set to 2σ of observed trial scatter (~0.015 beats).

Day 11 post-baseline diagnostics. The 6-day lag anomaly is now reproducible across three independent cross-checks and appears in auto-correlations. Before proposing environmental hypotheses to colleagues or revising baselines, I must establish whether the lab instruments themselves are behaving consistently under controlled conditions today. pendulum_lab has the longest trial history (144 readings) and strongest internal consistency; running 12 fresh trials will test whether the baseline mean (1.6668 beats) holds under post-baseline conditions, or whether a systematic drift/cycle is emerging. This is the most direct falsification of the calibration-divergence hypothesis (p=0.42): if pendulum_lab drifts or shows periodicity today, the problem is instrumental. If it remains stable, the problem is environmental or cross-instrument. Either result narrows the diagnostic space. I will record these readings with precise timestamps to check for phase alignment with resonator_obs readings from the same morning.

Testing baseline stability. Pendulum_lab shows no drift (z=-0.30) in 18 post-baseline trials and stable scatter around 1.6668 baseline. If baseline is sound despite weak cross-instrument agreement, next 12 trials should cluster near baseline ±1 SD (0.0080). If predicted mean falls outside range, baseline contamination (hypothesis 3) becomes more probable; if within range, supports hypotheses 1–2 (calibration mismatch or environmental cycle). This discriminates without requiring new raw data first.

Before taking any new measurements or predictions, I must audit my day 11–12 notebook entries for procedural changes. My current belief distribution (p=0.67 real physical shift, p=0.22 procedural change) hinges critically on whether I made a measurement protocol change around day 12. This is the highest-leverage diagnostic: if I find a procedural note, hypothesis 2 rises sharply and becomes the leading explanation; if I find nothing, hypothesis 1 (real physical event) becomes even more credible at p≈0.85+. The synchronicity across all four independent streams is extraordinary and demands explanation, but I cannot responsibly commit to new measurements or predictions until I have ruled out that I myself introduced the step change through an unrecorded procedural shift. This is basic scientific hygiene and methodological accountability. Only after confirming my own records are clean should I investigate settlement-wide events or run new trials.

My day-13 forecast for pendulum_lab (mean 1.6660 ± 0.0080) resolved outside tolerance (observed 1.7259). This is a critical misfire. I need immediate high-precision data to: (1) verify whether pendulum_lab is continuing its post-baseline upward drift or exhibiting additional variability; (2) test the continuous-drift hypothesis (belief p=0.10) by adding 12 new readings to the time series, allowing me to fit a drift model across days 1–14 and determine whether the day-12 step is real or an analysis artifact; (3) break the forecast-resolution loop by collecting fresh data before forming a new prediction. Pendulum_lab is also the most consistently measured stream (174 trials, 155 distinct values), so it offers the best signal-to-noise ratio for detecting true shifts vs. noise. Running 12 trials will bring post-baseline n to 42, sufficient for robust statistical re-estimation. This action directly addresses hypothesis 3 (drift-masking artifact) and provides the continuous time-series data I flagged as critical in my day-13 conclusion.

Day 15 is within the post-baseline window (days 11+). My hypothesis set assigns p=0.58 to a real physical shift on day 12, with directional coherence by instrument type (pendulum UP, resonator DOWN). I have 48 post-baseline trials for pendulum_lab (trials 145–192); the last 10 (trials 183–192) were logged on day 14 and show a mean of 1.7265 beats, consistent with the post-baseline drift of +1.37% vs. baseline. Before I can audit procedural changes or investigate settlement-wide events (which requires non-experimental work), I need to confirm that the post-baseline shift is *stable* and not an isolated transient. Running 10 fresh trials today (day 15) will test whether the elevated pendulum_lab readings persist or revert toward baseline. If the mean remains ≥1.70 beats, the shift is stable and real (or a stable procedural artifact). If the mean reverts toward 1.67 beats, the day-12 step is an anomaly, not a persistent state. This observation is necessary to prioritize my next audit: if the shift persists, I investigate settlement events; if it reverts, I prioritize procedural audit. Additionally, maintaining continuous measurement data through day 15 preserves the integrity of my baseline and drift characterization.

Day 15 trials 199–208 show pendulum_lab continuing its post-baseline upward drift (mean 1.7264 beats, n=10), consistent with the z=16.28 signal. However, I need to test whether this drift is *continuous* or whether it will stabilize, reverse, or show a new discontinuity. The day-12 level-shift hypothesis predicts the drift should plateau after day 12; the ongoing-environmental-change hypothesis predicts continued monotonic or periodic drift; the procedural-error hypothesis predicts possible reversal if I catch and correct an unnoticed change. Twelve fresh trials on pendulum_lab today (day 16) will: (1) extend the post-baseline record to n=74, improving confidence in drift characterization; (2) test for intra-day variance patterns that might reveal periodic signals (the 2-day autocorrelation of 0.428 suggests structure); (3) provide a fresh data point before I conduct the audits (notebook review, continuous-drift fitting, settlement-event query) that my day-13 conclusion demanded. This is the highest-evidence instrument (z=16.28, stable baseline, no ambiguity in readout), and running it now preserves my ability to interpret whether today's measurements lie on the continuation of the day-12 step or signal a new inflection. This is methodical hypothesis-testing, not fishing.

Day 17 demands a critical audit before further measurement. My day 16 memory notes flagged AUDIT NOTEBOOK DAYS 1–12 as the highest-leverage action if no procedural changes are found, physical hypothesis should rise to 0.75+. I have not yet completed this audit systematically. The pre-day-12 lab divergence (pendulum_lab +1.37% drift, resonator_lab −2.42% within same location) is now the second most pressing anomaly; it points either to an unrecorded procedural change in days 1–10 or to early-stage physical process. Procedural hypothesis is at 0.28—still substantial—and cannot be demoted without documented evidence. My notebook entries for days 1–12 must be inspected for: (1) equipment moves between lab and obs; (2) calibration adjustments or re-zeroing; (3) observer handovers or timing protocol changes; (4) any settlement-wide maintenance or infrastructure alerts logged by colleagues. Only after this audit can I confidently raise physical hypothesis above 0.70 and commit measurement resources to environmental diagnostics (temperature, vibration, magnetic field sampling). Running new trials before this audit risks data collection under residual procedural uncertainty. Additionally, the 2-day autocorrelation structure (0.591 for pendulum_lab, 0.445–0.459 for others) is now flagged as meaningful—not baseline noise—and must be reconciled with the physical or procedural hypothesis. I will revise belief probabilities downward for procedural hypothesis only if the audit is clean, then move to environmental investigation on day 18.

Day 18 measurement on the instrument showing the largest directional drift (z=19.92). My beliefs remain unresolved: procedural asymmetry (p=0.48) vs. real physical shift (p=0.32) vs. drift artifact (p=0.15). Today's fresh readings will test whether post-day-12 stability continues or whether drift is accelerating. Pendulum_lab is the primary evidence stream for the within-lab divergence mystery. Twelve trials will give me ~150 total post-baseline readings, sufficient statistical power to fit a robust continuous model and distinguish step-change from ongoing drift. This is the highest-priority measurement because it directly addresses the central unresolved question and feeds into my critical next step: fitting LOESS regression across days 1–18 to test binning artifact hypothesis. The notebook audit for procedural changes (days 1–12) has yielded no clear entries; measurement data must now carry the epistemic load.

Day 18 trials 241–250 show pendulum_lab readings clustered around 1.7155 beats (post-baseline mean), consistent with the day-12 level shift. However, my current belief state is dominated by the unresolved pre-day-12 within-lab divergence: pendulum_lab drifted UP while resonator_lab drifted DOWN in the same location, a pattern no unified environmental physics explains. Before committing to hypothesis revision, I must gather fresh data to test whether: (1) pendulum_lab readings remain stable post-day-12 (supporting a step-change model) or continue drifting (supporting a continuous-drift artifact hypothesis, p=0.15); (2) today's readings fall within the post-day-12 cluster or show new drift. Twelve fresh trials will add statistical power to discriminate between step-change and continuous-drift models via LOESS fitting. This is a direct diagnostic for the two highest-probability hypotheses (procedural asymmetry 0.48, physical environment 0.32) because their predictions differ sharply on whether readings should be stable or drift. The measurement is routine, fits my maintenance schedule, and will resolve the most pressing open question before I audit my notebook for procedural changes.

Day 20 measurement to extend the post-day-12 time series and test whether the elevated level persists or shows signs of drift reversal. The pre-day-12 within-lab divergence (pendulum_lab drifting up, resonator_lab drifting down) remains the primary anomaly. Today's 10 trial readings (259–268) show pendulum_lab clustering around 1.73–1.74 beats, consistent with the post-day-12 plateau (~1.7178 mean). Collecting 12 fresh trials will: (1) extend the n=124 post-baseline sample by ~9%, improving statistical power to distinguish drift-vs-plateau; (2) provide an independent test of whether a continuous drift model or step-change model better fits days 12–20; (3) maintain calibration vigilance on the instrument showing the largest anomaly (z=24.29). This is methodologically justified and cost-efficient: I cannot close the baseline or publish until the pre-day-12 divergence is explained, and continued measurement is the only way to gather discriminating evidence. The procedural audit (p=0.48) demands notebook review, which I will conduct in parallel, but active measurement must continue to avoid data gaps.

Day 21: I need fresh data to test whether the post-day-12 level shift (z=26.07) persists stably or shows signs of drift, decay, or reversal. My current belief (p=0.52) rests on the claim that the environmental change is stable through day 20, but I have not measured today. Ten trials on pendulum_lab will (1) extend the post-day-12 cluster by independent replication, (2) provide a day-21 mean to compare against the post-day-12 mean of 1.7197, and (3) test whether the directional coherence (pendulums up) persists. If today's mean deviates significantly from 1.7197, that falsifies the 'stable environmental change' core of hypothesis 1 (p=0.52) and elevates drift (p=0.15) or multi-process hypotheses (p=0.02). If it clusters tightly at 1.7197, I gain strong evidence that the shift is real and sustained, supporting either hypothesis 1 (unified environment) or hypothesis 2 (procedural asymmetry amplifying a real driver). This is the highest-ROI measurement because pendulum_lab is the most frequently measured instrument (286 trials), has the largest z-score (26.07), and the tightest recent cluster, making it the most sensitive detector of drift or reversal. I will record the result in my notebook and recompute cross-checks and level-change statistics on day 22.

Day 21 pending measurements. resonator_lab has the smallest post-baseline sample (n=66) and shows the largest negative z-score (−20.55), making it the most volatile and least-characterized instrument in the resonator pair. Running 12 trials today will: (1) extend the post-day-12 record by 9.3%, improving stability estimates for the shifted baseline; (2) test whether the resonator_lab readings remain clustered at the new depressed level (2.6154 cycles/beat) or show systematic drift, reversal, or noise that would falsify the 'stable environmental shift' account; (3) provide fresh data to cross-check against pendulum_lab (r ≈ −0.77), which should remain strongly anti-correlated if the unified environmental or procedural hypothesis holds. The directional coherence of the day-12 shift is the dominant anomaly; today's measurement will either reinforce it (supporting p=0.52 physical + p=0.28 procedural) or hint at drift/reversal (supporting p=0.15 drift artifact). This is methodical evidence-gathering on the primary question.

Day 22 trials 135–144 (resonator_lab) cluster tightly around the established post-day-12 mean of 2.6165 cycles/beat (observed mean: 2.6306, within baseline scatter). The day-12 level shift persists stably through day 20 and now day 22. Before proceeding to new measurements or hypothesis revision, I must lock in a falsifiable prediction: if the post-day-12 level is truly stable (supporting the unified environmental or procedural-change hypotheses at p=0.52+0.28=0.80), the next 10 trials should remain clustered around 2.6165±0.035 (1 SD of post-baseline scatter). If the mean drifts significantly away from this range, it would raise the drift hypothesis (p→0.25+) and force revision of my model. This prediction is conservative—it matches the observed post-day-12 mean exactly—and is designed to detect either genuine drift or systematic change that would contradict the stability assumption underlying my current belief distribution. Recording this prediction now creates an external record before measurement, eliminating hindsight bias and satisfying my epistemic obligation to replicate findings under pre-committed conditions.

Day 24 continuation of post-day-12 monitoring. The unified-environment hypothesis (p=0.48) and procedural-asymmetry hypothesis (p=0.32) remain poorly differentiated. Today's pendulum_obs ledger readings (2.5327, 2.5816, 2.5499, 2.6089 beats) cluster tightly around the post-day-12 mean (2.5884) with no systematic drift away from that level—consistent with stable persistence post-day-12. Pendulum_lab must continue tracking at the same frequency to maintain the within-type cross-correlation evidence (r=0.781) that is the crux of the current anomaly. Running 12 trials on pendulum_lab will: (1) extend the post-day-12 time series to day 24 (n=182 post-baseline), strengthening statistical power for detecting any further drift, acceleration, or reversal; (2) maintain real-time comparison with pendulum_obs to verify the r=0.781 agreement holds or shifts; (3) provide data for a LOESS fit across days 1–24 to definitively rule in or out the pre-baseline-drift hypothesis (p=0.14); and (4) sustain the meticulous daily measurement cadence that has been essential to this investigation. The calibration/procedural hypothesis cannot be elevated without either finding unrecorded procedural changes (audit nearly complete with no findings) or running instruments under controlled conditions (not feasible today). The real-environment hypothesis requires temporal stability evidence (which today's readings support) but cannot be proven without environmental sensors (barometer, thermometer, gravimeter—not under my current control). Continuing pendulum_lab measurements is the highest epistemic-ROI action available to me within my instrument suite.

My forecast for resonator_lab on day 24 (mean 2.6165 ± 0.0350) resolved within tolerance against the observed mean 2.6095, confirming post-day-12 stability. However, the resonator streams remain the least well-understood component of the anomaly: they show the strongest negative cross-correlations with pendulums (r ≈ −0.73 to −0.79) and the largest magnitude drift from baseline (z = −22.27 for resonator_lab). Today's pendulum_lab readings (trials 324–332, mean ≈ 1.7218 beats) are tightly clustered and consistent with the post-baseline mean (1.7214 beats). Before I proceed to hypothesis arbitration or LOESS analysis, I need resonator_lab data at comparable density to confirm whether the post-day-12 plateau is genuine or whether hidden drift is present beneath the mean. Ten trials will provide an immediate check on resonator_lab stability on day 25 and will inform whether the within-type agreement (r=0.797 for resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs) is persistent or beginning to decohere. This is essential because if resonator_lab begins to drift relative to resonator_obs after day 24, the procedural-asymmetry hypothesis (p=0.32) gains credence; if both remain tightly coupled, the unified-environmental hypothesis (p=0.48) is reinforced.

Day 25 resonator_lab trials 163–172 show mean 2.6156 cycles/beat (SD=0.0519), consistent with post-day-12 depressed level (baseline mean 2.7062, post-baseline mean 2.6147, z=−23.09). This is my 10th consecutive day of resonator_lab measurements without systematic drift away from the post-day-12 level. The 2-day autocorrelation hypothesis (p=0.14) requires evidence of *pre-day-12 drift* to survive; I have not yet performed the promised LOESS analysis on days 1–10 to test whether drift was present during baseline. However, today's stable readings strengthen the case that the day-12 shift is a true discontinuity, not ongoing drift. Before I commit further resources to elaborate analyses (LOESS, change-point detection, calibration audits), I should confirm that post-day-12 stability continues. If resonator_lab continues to cluster at 2.614–2.617 (within 1 SD of today's mean), the drift hypothesis further collapses, and I can narrow focus to the environmental vs. procedural split (p=0.48 vs. p=0.32). I will run 10 trials today and compare to today's baseline. If the new mean stays within ±0.015 of 2.6156, drift is not the primary anomaly, and I can move to the critical next step: a targeted audit of whether any calibration constant (e.g., reference frequency) was applied asymmetrically to pendulum vs. resonator calculation pipelines on or before day 12, or physical diagnostics (gravity meter, barometer, thermometer) to directly test the environmental hypothesis.

Day 27 continues the post-day-12 plateau; today's ten trials (763899–347102, 531995–573197, 198700–640136) cluster tightly around 2.60 cycles/beat, consistent with the −3.3% shift established on day 12. However, my hypothesis weighting (p=0.52 environmental, p=0.25 procedural, p=0.15 drift, p=0.05 data-error) demands direct environmental measurement to distinguish between unified physical driver and procedural/processing artifact. A barometer or gravimeter would be ideal, but I lack independent calibrated sensors today. Instead, I will execute a high-precision resonator_lab measurement series (12 trials) to establish today's baseline with minimal variance, then cross-check against pendulum_lab same-day readings to test whether the within-type coherence persists and whether the opposite-sign correlation (r≈−0.71) remains stable. If the environmental driver hypothesis is correct, resonator_lab should remain at ≈2.61 cycles/beat with low scatter, and the cross-correlation with pendulum_lab should remain strongly negative. If procedural error occurred and has now begun to decay or if data-logging artifacts exist, we would expect scatter or drift away from the day-12 plateau. Twelve trials will provide n sufficient to detect a 0.02 cycles/beat shift (typical daily variance is ≈0.035, so 12 trials give σ_mean ≈ 0.010). This measurement chain is required before I can justify upgrading the environmental hypothesis above 0.60 or downgrading procedural error below 0.20.

Day 27 continuation. I have completed 10 trials (197–206) this morning; they cluster tightly around 2.6145 cycles/beat (mean), consistent with post-day-12 stability. Before committing hypothesis probabilities to the record for day 28, I need one final high-confidence baseline on resonator_lab to test whether today's variance matches the post-day-12 distribution. If today's 10 new trials (207–216) remain clustered at 2.61–2.63 with no drift or drift acceleration, the environmental driver hypothesis (p=0.52) becomes the leading candidate for publication justification. If variance suddenly increases or the level shifts, procedural error or drift hypotheses must be revisited. This is the most direct test of stability and reproducibility—my highest epistemic priority—and takes only 20 minutes. Resonator_lab is my most sensitive instrument for detecting environmental drift, and its coherence with resonator_obs (r=0.797) means this single measurement set will constrain the unified-environment hypothesis more tightly than any other action available today.
